Difficulty: Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 appear to tell the creation story twice, and in a different order. In Genesis 1, plants appear on day three, animals on days five and six, and man and woman together at the end, after the animals. In Genesis 2, man is formed first, then the garden is planted, then the animals are formed and brought to the man, and only then is woman made from the man's side. If both chapters are straightforward chronological reports, they seem to contradict each other about what came first: plants or man, animals or man, man or woman.
Explanations: The widely shared reading is that the two chapters do different jobs and are not both running on the same timeline. Genesis 1 is a broad, ordered panorama of the whole creation week, ending with humanity as its crown. Genesis 2 zooms in on the sixth day and retells it topically, filling in the garden, the man's work, the naming of the animals, and the making of the woman, without claiming that each event in chapter 2 happened after the previous one in strict sequence. On this reading, the Hebrew narrative style allows a topical retelling to sit beside an ordered overview, and the 'forming' of animals in Genesis 2:19 can be read as a flashback to their creation rather than a second creation after the man. A minority literal-chronological reading tries to harmonise every verb in sequence, but the topical reading is the one most commentators adopt, because Genesis 2 itself signals its narrower focus by opening with 'these are the generations of the heavens and of the earth' and then concentrating on the garden.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that the two accounts are complementary, not contradictory: Genesis 1 gives the wide ordered account and Genesis 2 gives the close-up, human-centred account of the same creation. This row settles only the order question; it does not settle how long the 'days' of Genesis 1 were, which remains a separate debate covered by the existing question 'Did God create the world in six literal days?'

Difficulty: Genesis 6:6 says 'it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.' Yet Numbers 23:19 says God 'is not a man, that he should repent,' and other passages insist God does not change his mind the way people do. Taken at face value, the two claims collide: either God does change his mind, and the denial passages are wrong, or he does not, and Genesis 6 is misleading about what God felt and did.
Explanations: The standard resolution turns on the Hebrew word behind 'repented' and on the kind of language being used. The word (nacham) covers grief, sorrow, and a change of course in response to changed circumstances, not only the human experience of admitting a mistake. Genesis 6 uses vivid, relational language: God grieves over human wickedness as a person grieves, and his dealings with humanity take a new course in judgment and then in preservation through Noah. Numbers 23:19, by contrast, is about God's covenant faithfulness: unlike a human ruler, he does not lie, break a promise, or reverse a settled purpose because of pressure or new information. On this reading both statements are true at different levels: God's character and promises do not waver, while his expressed responses within history genuinely reflect the changing state of his creatures. A related passage, Exodus 32:14, where God 'repented of the evil' he had threatened against Israel after Moses interceded, is treated in the existing question 'Does prayer change God's mind?' rather than as a separate row here.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 'God repented' in Genesis 6 is sorrowful, relational language describing God's real grief and his changed dealings with a wicked generation, not a claim that God discovered a mistake or abandoned a promise. The denial in Numbers 23:19 guards God's faithfulness, and the two passages answer different questions.

Passage: Where Did Cain's Wife Come From?
Difficulty: After Cain kills Abel, Genesis 4:17 says Cain 'knew his wife; and she conceived.' But the story so far has named only Adam, Eve, Cain, and Abel. If Adam and Eve were the first humans and their children were the only people on earth, there seems to be nobody for Cain to marry, and nobody to populate the city he is said to build. Readers reasonably ask whether the text has quietly assumed other people outside the family, which would sit awkwardly with Adam as the first man.
Explanations: The usual answer reads Genesis 4 together with Genesis 5:4, which says Adam 'begat sons and daughters' over a long life. Cain's wife, on this reading, was a sister or other close female relative, born to Adam and Eve but not named in the compressed early narrative, which names only the children who matter to the storyline. Early in human history, before the later law forbidding close marriage and before the accumulation of harmful genetic effects that such laws also guard against, marriage within the family was the only possibility and is not presented as a moral problem in the text. The city Cain builds is likewise not evidence of a large outside population: in ancient usage a small fortified settlement, built over time by a growing family, could carry the name. An alternative suggestion, that God created other humans alongside Adam, has little support in the text itself, which traces all humanity to the one pair and treats Cain's line as part of that family.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that the text gives no reason to invent a second human origin: Cain married a relative from Adam and Eve's wider family, unnamed because Genesis names only storyline figures at this point. The passage is silent about her identity, and that silence is a gap in detail, not a contradiction.
RelatedTopics: Genealogy; Family; Marriage; The Fall; Humanity; Biblical Interpretation

Difficulty: Jacob, helped by his mother Rebekah, disguises himself as Esau, lies to his blind father Isaac, and takes the blessing meant for his elder brother. God had already said the elder would serve the younger, but Jacob gets there by fraud, and the blessing, once spoken, cannot be taken back. Readers stumble twice over: first, does God reward cheating, since Jacob goes on to become the father of Israel? And second, does the story make deception acceptable when it serves a promised outcome?
Explanations: Commentators widely agree on two points that keep the story from endorsing the trick. First, the narrative never praises the deception: Isaac trembles when he discovers it, Esau weeps, and Jacob pays for years, fleeing for his life, being tricked in turn by Laban over his own wives, and living in fear of Esau's revenge. The consequences are woven through the following chapters as the story's own judgment on the method. Second, God's purpose and human scheming are kept distinct: the promise that the elder would serve the younger was given before the twins were born, and the story shows God working his purpose out even through flawed people, not because of their flaws. Rebekah's earlier scheme, Esau's casual sale of his birthright, and Isaac's attempt to bless the son he favoured are all shown as human grasping around a promise God had already made.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Genesis 27 describes deception and its bitter costs; it does not commend it. God's promise to Jacob stands in spite of the trick, not because the trick was good, and the chapters that follow are best read as the price Jacob paid for taking the blessing by hand rather than waiting for God to give it.
RelatedTopics: Covenant; God's Sovereignty; God's promises; Sin; Family; Ethics; Moral Responsibility

Passage: No One Can See God's Face, Yet They Saw God
Difficulty: God tells Moses, 'Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.' Yet the same book says Moses spoke with God 'face to face' (Exodus 33:11), that the elders of Israel 'saw the God of Israel' on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:9-11), and Jacob earlier claimed, 'I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved' (Genesis 32:30). Either seeing God is fatal, and these reports are impossible, or it is not, and the warning to Moses is empty.
Explanations: The resolution most readers adopt distinguishes between seeing God's full, unveiled glory and seeing a mediated, accommodated appearance of God. In Exodus 33 itself, God offers Moses a middle way: Moses will see God's 'back parts' as his glory passes by, sheltered in the cleft of the rock, because the full sight would be more than a mortal can bear. The other 'seeings' are of the same accommodated kind: a visible manifestation, a form, a presence on the mountain, described in human language because human language has nothing else to use. The 'face to face' of Exodus 33:11 is explained by its own context as the intimacy of the conversation, like friends speaking, not as a claim that Moses stared at God's essence. Later Scripture keeps the same distinction, insisting no one has seen God in his fullness while also recording appearances of God in forms people could survive.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that there is no contradiction once the distinction is kept: no mortal survives an unveiled sight of God's glory, and every biblical 'seeing' of God is a gracious, veiled manifestation suited to human limits. The warning to Moses is the rule that explains the other passages, not a rival to them.

Difficulty: The sixth commandment in the King James Version reads, 'Thou shalt not kill.' Yet the same law of Moses commands capital punishment, authorises warfare, and permits killing in self-defence and in defence of the home. If all killing is forbidden, then God contradicts his own commandment within a few chapters. If it is not, then the most famous wording of the commandment seems to mislead ordinary readers, and pacifist and non-pacifist Christians alike need to know what it actually forbids.
Explanations: This is a translation point, and it is widely settled. The Hebrew verb used here (ratsach) does not mean killing in general; it means unlawful killing, the taking of innocent life, what modern translations render as 'murder.' The commandment therefore forbids murder, not every act that ends a life: the same legal code that contains it goes on to distinguish deliberate murder from accidental killing, to provide cities of refuge for the accidental killer, and to prescribe death as a judicial penalty for certain crimes. Whether Christians today should support capital punishment or any particular war is a separate moral argument, but it is not decided by pretending this verse bans all killing; the verse's own context in the law shows it never meant that.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Exodus 20:13 forbids murder, the unlawful taking of innocent life, and that the King James wording 'kill' should be read with that narrower Hebrew sense. The apparent clash with the law's own penalties dissolves once the verb is translated accurately.
RelatedTopics: Christian Ethics; Morality; Justice; Violence; Translation; Scripture; Word of God
Sources: On-site KJV text of Exodus 20:13 and the surrounding legal material; general Hebrew word-study discussion of ratsach. No single source relied on or cited.

Difficulty: 'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot' sounds like a charter for revenge: injure me and I may injure you back in exactly the same way. That reading clashes with the Bible's own calls to mercy and forgiveness, and with Jesus' teaching to turn the other cheek. Readers wonder whether the law of Moses really licensed personal vengeance, and if so, how it can belong to the same moral world as the rest of Scripture.
Explanations: The scholarly consensus about the original function of this law is that it limited vengeance rather than licensing it. In a world where a lost eye could be repaid with a life, or a clan feud could run for generations, the formula set a ceiling: the penalty must match the injury, no more. It was also a judicial rule, administered by judges, not a permission slip for the injured party to take revenge in person; the surrounding passage is a courtroom scale of compensation for injuries, and later Jewish practice generally applied it as monetary compensation equal to the value of the loss. Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount then addresses personal retaliation and goes beyond the judicial minimum toward non-retaliation, which is a deepening of the ethic, not a correction of a bloodthirsty rule. The law's own point was proportionality and restraint.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 'eye for eye' was a restraint on revenge, not a command to take it: a judge's rule that punishment must fit the injury and never exceed it. Read in its courtroom context, it points toward the same justice that later teaching carries further into mercy, rather than against it.
RelatedTopics: Justice; Christian Ethics; Morality; Forgiveness; Mercy; Judgment

Difficulty: Leviticus forbids eating pork, shellfish, and other creatures, bans mixing kinds of seed and cloth, and calls all of it part of God's law. Yet Christians eat pork and wear mixed fabrics without a second thought. If God's law is God's law, why do Christians ignore whole chapters of it? And if these rules were never about morality at all, why did God give them in such detail, and why do some Christians still appeal to Leviticus on other questions, such as sexual ethics, while setting the food laws aside?
Explanations: The widely shared explanation is that these laws marked Israel out as a distinct, holy people under the old covenant, not that they stated timeless moral rules for all people. Food, farming, and clothing rules functioned as daily boundary markers: every meal and every garment reminded Israel it belonged to God and was set apart from surrounding nations. That is why the New Testament can describe the food laws as fulfilled and set aside for Gentile believers while still treating the moral commands of the law, such as love of neighbour and prohibitions on murder and theft, as enduring. The distinction is sometimes labelled ceremonial versus moral law; scholars debate how tidy that labelling is, and where exactly each command falls, but there is broad agreement on the core point, that the identity-marker function of the clean and unclean code belonged to Israel's covenant situation. Appeals to Leviticus on other questions therefore have to argue, case by case, whether a given command is an identity marker or a moral rule, rather than assuming all of Leviticus stands or falls together.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that the clean and unclean laws were covenant identity markers for Israel, not universal moral law, and that Christians are not bound by them as food or clothing rules. The harder question, which command in Leviticus is moral and which is a marker, has to be argued passage by passage, and this row does not settle every such case by itself.
RelatedTopics: Holiness; Purity; Covenant; Christian Ethics; Biblical Interpretation; Worship; Temple

Difficulty: After Israel complains in the wilderness, God sends fiery serpents, and many die. Then God tells Moses to make a serpent of brass, set it on a pole, and promises that anyone bitten who looks at it will live. The difficulty is sharp: the second commandment forbids making a graven image, and this looks exactly like one, a metal serpent used as a means of healing. Worse, the same object later becomes an idol, Nehushtan, that King Hezekiah has to destroy. Did God command idolatry and then punish it?
Explanations: The distinction drawn by most readers is between an image made and used at God's command as a means of grace, and an image worshipped as a god. The bronze serpent was not worshipped in Numbers 21; it was looked at in obedient trust toward God's promise, and the healing came from God, not from the metal. The object itself was neutral, a God-appointed sign pointing sufferers away from themselves and toward God's mercy. That is also why its later fate makes sense rather than contradicting the story: centuries later, when Israelites were burning incense to it as if it had power in itself, Hezekiah broke it in pieces, calling it a mere thing of brass. The same object was legitimate as a sign and illegitimate as an idol, and the difference lay in how it was treated. The New Testament later uses the lifted-up serpent as a picture of Christ lifted up, which fits the sign reading: the serpent pointed beyond itself.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that the bronze serpent was a commanded sign, not a sanctioned idol: looking at it in faith was obedience to God's word, while burning incense to it later was idolatry. The passage warns against worshipping the means of grace rather than the God who gives it.
RelatedTopics: Idolatry; Miracles; Faith; God's mercy; Worship; True Worship; Wilderness

Difficulty: Deuteronomy 5 repeats the Ten Commandments, but not word for word. The wording differs in places from Exodus 20, and the reason given for the Sabbath changes: Exodus grounds it in God's rest after creation, while Deuteronomy grounds it in Israel's deliverance from Egypt ('remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt'). If both are God's own words, delivered on Sinai, why do they differ? Either one version is inaccurate, or the claim that God spoke these words needs qualifying.
Explanations: The standard explanation is that Deuteronomy is a covenant renewal sermon, not a second transcript. Moses is addressing a new generation on the edge of the promised land, restating the law for its situation, and restatement in preaching naturally uses fresh wording and draws out a fresh motive. The two Sabbath reasons are complementary, not competing: creation gives the pattern of rest, and the exodus gives Israel's own experience of why rest matters, since slaves in Egypt had no rest. Ancient legal restatement worked the same way, applying and expounding a law for a new setting rather than photocopying it. The differences are therefore exactly what one would expect from a preached republication, and the shared core, the same ten commands in the same order, shows a stable law being re-applied, not two rival laws.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Deuteronomy 5 is Moses' faithful restatement of the Sinai law for a new generation, and the wording differences, including the two Sabbath motives, are complementary exposition rather than contradiction. Neither version needs to be treated as a verbatim transcript to be trustworthy.

Difficulty: Deuteronomy ends with Moses' death, his burial by God, and a survey of his whole life: 'there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses.' If Moses wrote Deuteronomy, he cannot have written the account of his own death and its aftermath. The passage is often taken as proof that Moses did not write the Pentateuch at all, and that the traditional ascription of the books to him collapses.
Explanations: The widely accepted resolution is modest: the bulk of Deuteronomy can be Moses' teaching while its final chapter is a postscript added after his death, traditionally ascribed to Joshua, who succeeds him in the very next book. Ancient books did not carry the modern expectation that every word, including a closing obituary, must come from the named author's hand; a disciple or successor completing the record was normal. The chapter itself reads like an obituary, praising Moses from a standpoint after his life is complete, which fits a successor's hand. This does not by itself settle larger questions about the composition history of the Pentateuch, on which scholars disagree, but the death notice alone does not disprove Mosaic authorship of the teaching it closes, any more than a biography's final chapter disproves that its subject wrote the letters quoted in it.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Deuteronomy 34 is best read as a postscript to Moses' work, added after his death, and that it poses no contradiction to the tradition that the teaching of Deuteronomy is Moses'. Wider composition questions are left open here rather than settled by this one chapter.

Passage: The Gibeonites' Trick and Israel's Oath
Difficulty: The Gibeonites deceive Israel by posing as travellers from a far country, and Israel's leaders swear a covenant of peace without asking the LORD first. Readers ask why a treaty obtained by fraud should bind Israel at all, and why God would honour an oath made on false pretences.
Explanations: One explanation stresses covenant ethics: in Israel's world a sworn oath was binding even when costly, and breaking such an oath later (2 Samuel 21) brought guilt on the land. Another stresses where the blame lies: the failure was in not seeking counsel, and the Gibeonites' servitude as woodcutters and water carriers was the imposed consequence. A third notes the Gibeonites had heard of the LORD's deeds and sought mercy, so the outcome is read as grace within judgment rather than approval of their deception.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The oath binds because Israel swore it, and the passage's blame falls on leaders who did not inquire of the LORD, not on keeping a sworn word. Deception explains how the treaty happened; it does not dissolve it.

Difficulty: The verse says the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah 'could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.' Read carelessly, it sounds as if God Himself were stopped by superior military technology.
Explanations: The standard grammatical reading resolves the tension: the subject who 'could not' is Judah, not the LORD. The LORD's presence is affirmed in the first half of the verse; Judah's failure in the second half is a human failure of nerve, obedience or persistence, of the kind Judges repeatedly attributes to Israel's incomplete conquest. No reading requires an impotent God, and the chapter's pattern is partial obedience, not divine defeat.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The text does not say God was defeated by chariots. It says Judah, though accompanied by the LORD, did not finish the task — a distinction the grammar and the chapter's theme both support.

Difficulty: Gideon twice asks God for a sign with a wool fleece — dry fleece on wet ground, then wet fleece on dry ground. Readers wonder whether this licenses 'putting out a fleece' as a normal way of making decisions, and whether Gideon was right to test God after already receiving a sign.
Explanations: Most readings agree Gideon is not presented as a model here. He has already been called, given a sign (Judges 6:17-24) and promised the LORD's presence; the fleece is a further plea from fear, which God graciously answers rather than rebukes at this point. The narrative function is to strengthen a fearful deliverer before battle, not to teach a decision-making technique — and later Scripture warns against testing God as a habit, while commending His already-given word and wisdom.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Gideon's fleece is best read as God's patience with a fearful man, not as a method to copy. A Christian with a clear command, wise counsel and an open Bible does not need a fleece, and should not demand one.

Difficulty: A Levite hands his concubine over to a mob, she is abused through the night and dies, and he then cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel. Readers ask, with full force, how such horror can be in Scripture, and whether the text in any way excuses the men involved.
Explanations: The widely agreed reading is that the passage is descriptive, not prescriptive: it is told as an indictment, not an endorsement. Its refrain — 'in those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes' (Judges 21:25) — frames the whole closing section as a portrait of a society collapsing into depravity, and the Levite himself is shown as callous and self-protecting, not heroic. The shock is the point: Israel needs righteous rule, and the reader is meant to recoil, not imitate.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: This passage condemns by exposure. Nothing in it praises the Levite, the mob or the tribe that sheltered them, and reading it as approval would invert the narrator's own verdict.

Difficulty: After the civil war against Benjamin, Israel first swears not to give its daughters to Benjamin, then sanctions the killing of Jabesh-gilead's men so their virgins can be given as wives, and finally tells the surviving Benjaminites to seize dancing girls at Shiloh. Readers ask how a book of Scripture can report kidnapping as a solution.
Explanations: As with Judges 19, the agreed reading is descriptive indictment. The chapter shows leaders solving one oath-bound disaster with two further wrongs, each justified by expediency rather than by God's law. The book closes on the same refrain — no king, every man doing what is right in his own eyes — which signals that the narrator regards the whole sequence as moral collapse, not as a divinely approved precedent.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The seizure of wives is presented as the last failure in a chain of failures, not as God's will. The passage's darkness is its argument: Israel's anarchy is intolerable and needs a king after God's heart.

Difficulty: Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor at night, where Ruth lies at Boaz's feet and asks him to spread his skirt over her. Modern readers easily hear sexual impropriety in the scene, and wonder whether Ruth was compromising herself or Boaz was taking advantage.
Explanations: The cultural reading, widely agreed, is that Ruth's request uses the language of protection and marriage (the 'skirt' or cloak as a symbol of a kinsman-redeemer's covering), not seduction. Boaz's response — blessing her, refusing to act until the nearer kinsman has his right, sending her home before dawn so no scandal attaches, and settling the matter publicly at the gate the next day — is presented as honourable restraint. Nothing in the text implies a sexual encounter; the scene's tension is legal and social, resolved in daylight and in public.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Read in its own culture, the threshing-floor scene is a chaste, lawful appeal for redemption, and Boaz's conduct is the passage's model of restraint, not its violation.

Passage: Saul's Age and Reign in 1 Samuel 13:1
Difficulty: The KJV reads: 'Saul reigned one year; and when he had reigned two years over Israel.' The verse as it stands is unintelligible as a reign length, since Saul plainly reigns far longer, and the Hebrew text behind it is evidently defective at exactly this point.
Explanations: Textual critics agree the Hebrew numbers here have been lost or corrupted in transmission: the verse lacks the figure for Saul's age at accession and one figure is incomplete. Ancient versions and later manuscripts differ in their attempts to fill the gap, which is itself evidence that no original reading survived intact in the Masoretic tradition. The passage is therefore a copyist problem, not a historical claim that Saul reigned only two years, and no doctrine turns on the missing numbers.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The honest reading is that 1 Samuel 13:1 is a damaged verse whose numbers cannot be recovered with certainty. That is a fact about transmission, not a contradiction between two complete statements.

Difficulty: 1 Samuel 31 says Saul, wounded by archers, fell on his own sword, and his armour-bearer did the same. In 2 Samuel 1 an Amalekite tells David he finished Saul off at Saul's request. The two accounts cannot both be literal history as told, so readers ask which is true.
Explanations: The agreed reading treats the narrator's account in 1 Samuel 31 as the event, and the Amalekite's story as self-serving fabrication. The Amalekite arrives with Saul's crown and bracelet — plunder he could have taken from the corpse — and has an obvious motive: to win favour with David as Saul's successor. David himself treats the claim as a confession of killing the LORD's anointed and executes him, which makes sense whether or not David believed him, since claiming the deed was itself the crime. The tension is therefore between a reliable narrator and an unreliable character, not between two narrators.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Saul died by his own hand on Mount Gilboa, as 1 Samuel 31 narrates. The Amalekite's version is best read as a lie told for reward, and David's judgment falls on the claim itself.

Difficulty: In the same chapter God says, 'It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king,' and Samuel then declares that 'the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.' Readers ask how both can be true, and whether God changes His mind.
Explanations: The standard explanation is that Scripture speaks of God in human terms when it describes His grief and His changed dealings with a person whose conduct has changed. God's settled purpose and character do not change; what changes is the relationship and the outcome, because Saul has changed. 'Repent' in verse 11 describes God's sorrow and His reversal of Saul's kingship; 'will not repent' in verse 29 denies that God is fickle or can be talked out of His settled judgment, as a man might be.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The two verses speak at different levels: God grieves and responds to human change, and God does not waver like a man. There is no contradiction once the human language of verse 11 is read as Scripture itself glosses it in verse 29.

Difficulty: The Hebrew text gives Goliath's height as six cubits and a span — roughly nine feet nine inches — while the Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript give four cubits and a span, roughly six feet nine inches. Readers ask which is right, and whether the difference undermines the story.
Explanations: Textual evidence points to a genuine variant in transmission: the Hebrew tradition and the Greek tradition preserve different figures, and scholars differ on which direction the change went, but agree a variant exists. Either way the narrative point is untouched: Goliath is presented as a giant champion towering over Israel's soldiers, and David's victory depends on God, not on the exact measurement. No theological claim rests on the number of cubits.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Goliath's exact height cannot be settled from the surviving manuscripts alone, and does not need to be. The variant is a textual footnote, not a crack in the story's meaning.

Difficulty: Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, then hates and discards her; Absalom murders Amnon in revenge; David, though angry, does nothing. Readers ask why Scripture includes sexual violence at the heart of David's house, and why David's passivity goes unpunished in the chapter.
Explanations: The agreed reading is descriptive: the chapter is part of Nathan's announced consequence — 'the sword shall never depart from thine house' (2 Samuel 12:10) — working itself out in David's own family. Tamar is given voice and dignity in the text (her protest, her torn robe, her ashes), Amnon's lust is named as hatred after the act, and Absalom's revenge, though understandable as a brother's anger, starts a rebellion that will tear the kingdom. David's failure to act is itself presented as a failure, with catastrophic consequences, not as something God overlooks.

Passage: Who Killed Goliath — David or Elhanan?

Difficulty: 1 Kings 4:26 credits Solomon with forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots; 2 Chronicles 9:25 gives four thousand stalls. Both agree on twelve thousand horsemen, so readers ask which stall figure is right.
Explanations: Numerals are the most easily corrupted element in hand-copied Hebrew texts, and this is a textbook case: a small difference turns four thousand into forty thousand. The Chronicles figure is also internally more plausible alongside twelve thousand horsemen. The discrepancy is therefore assigned to copyist transmission, not to two different Solomons or two different counts, and the passage's point — Solomon's vast, horse-rich kingdom — is the same on either figure.

Passage: The Molten Sea: Two Thousand or Three Thousand Baths?
Difficulty: The molten sea in the temple is said to contain two thousand baths in 1 Kings 7:26 but to receive and hold three thousand baths in 2 Chronicles 4:5. Readers ask whether the same vessel can have two capacities.

Passage: Manasseh's Repentance: Kings Silent, Chronicles Full
Difficulty: 2 Kings 21 describes Manasseh as Judah's worst king — idolatry, child sacrifice, innocent blood — with no mention of repentance. 2 Chronicles 33 adds that Manasseh was taken to Babylon in fetters, humbled himself, prayed, and was restored to Jerusalem, where he removed idols. Readers ask whether Chronicles invented a happy ending or Kings suppressed one.
Explanations: The two books have different purposes and selections, and neither claims to be exhaustive. Kings, written to explain the exile, stresses the guilt that made judgment inevitable; Chronicles, written to the returned exiles, stresses that even the worst king could repent and be restored — a message its audience needed. An omission in Kings is not a denial, and Chronicles' addition is consistent with the pattern of humbled kings elsewhere. The accounts overlap on Manasseh's crimes and his reign length; they differ in what each chose to include.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Kings and Chronicles are complementary, not contradictory, on Manasseh. Kings tells why judgment came; Chronicles tells that repentance was still possible, even for him.

Passage: The Return Lists: Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7
Difficulty: The two lists of returned exiles agree in their grand total — 42,360 — but differ in many individual family numbers, for example the children of Arah: 775 in Ezra 2:5 against 652 in Nehemiah 7:10. Readers ask why inspired lists cannot agree on their own arithmetic.
Explanations: The lists are not two independent censuses taken on the same day. Nehemiah 7 says explicitly that he found 'a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first' — that is, he is copying an older document, and the two copies have travelled through different transmission histories, where numerals corrupt most easily. Some differences may also reflect counting at different stages (those who set out, those who arrived, those registered later). The agreement on the total, alongside divergence in details, is exactly what copied registers look like.

Difficulty: Ezra 4 interrupts the story of the temple rebuilding under Cyrus with letters to later kings — Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes — complaining about Jerusalem's walls, then returns to the temple under Darius. Readers ask whether Ezra has muddled his kings and his chronology.

The letters themselves are genuine in form — Persian administrative correspondence — but their placement is editorial, grouping like with like rather than following the calendar.

Passage: A Book That Never Names God
Difficulty: The book of Esther never once mentions God, the LORD, prayer by name, or the law by name — unique among the Bible's historical books. Readers ask whether a God-less book belongs in Scripture, and whether its story is merely a secular court tale.
Explanations: The agreed reading is that God's absence from the vocabulary is the book's theology, not its defect. Providence works through 'coincidence': Esther's rise, Mordecai's overheard plot, the king's sleepless night, the gallows built for Mordecai used for Haman. Mordecai's own words — 'who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' (Esther 4:14) and his confidence that 'enlargement and deliverance' will arise 'from another place' — point to a hidden deliverer without naming Him. The book shows God working where He is not named, which is how many readers experience Him.

Passage: Why Could the Edict Not Be Revoked?
Difficulty: When Haman's genocidal edict is exposed, the king does not simply cancel it. Instead Mordecai must write a second edict permitting the Jews to defend themselves. Readers ask why a king who could order a massacre could not order its cancellation.
Explanations: The passage itself gives the reason, and Persian practice confirms it: 'the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse' (Esther 8:8). An irrevocable edict could be countered but not withdrawn, so the counter-edict — authorising self-defence and the plunder of attackers — was the legal remedy available. The narrative's tension depends on this rule: Haman's law stands, and deliverance must come through a second law rather than a royal change of mind.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The king could not revoke his sealed edict under Persian law, so a counter-edict was the lawful path to deliverance. The detail is historically coherent, not a plot hole.

Passage: Answer a Fool — and Do Not Answer a Fool
Difficulty: Verses 4 and 5 sit side by side and appear to give opposite commands. Verse 4 says, 'Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.' Verse 5 says, 'Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.' A reader who treats each proverb as a universal rule is left with a flat contradiction: whichever verse is obeyed, the other is broken.
Explanations: The pair is read as a matched set, not as two rival rules. Proverbs are situational wisdom, not unconditional promises or laws: each verse names a different danger and a different occasion. Verse 4 warns against descending to a fool's terms — arguing on his ground, with his methods — so that the answerer becomes like him. Verse 5 warns against silence that lets a fool's conceit stand unchallenged. The skill is in judging which danger the moment presents: sometimes engagement only feeds the folly, and silence is wiser; sometimes a brief, truthful answer is needed so folly is not mistaken for wisdom. The two verses together train discernment rather than prescribing one move for every encounter.
SiteAssessment: Site position: this is a genre resolution, not a contradiction. Proverbs 26:4-5 is deliberately paired teaching about when to speak and when to stay silent, and neither verse should be quoted alone as a blanket rule for every argument.

Passage: Train Up a Child — a Promise or a Principle?
Difficulty: 'Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.' Parents who raised a child in faith and watched that child walk away hear this as a broken promise, and some blame themselves entirely; others hear it used to guarantee an outcome no parent can control. The difficulty is real: stated flatly, the verse sounds like a guarantee, and experience supplies many exceptions.
Explanations: The widely agreed reading rests on genre. A proverb states a general pattern of how life usually works, not an unconditional divine promise: early training ordinarily shapes a life's direction, and the bent given in childhood tends to persist. It is not a contract that faithful parenting produces faithful adults without fail, and Scripture itself supplies counter-examples of godly parents with wayward children and wayward parents with godly children. The verse's force is therefore encouragement to diligent, early formation, not a verdict on any particular parent or child. A minority pastoral caution adds that 'the way he should go' may also carry the sense of the child's own bent or gifting, which would make the verse about fitting training to the child rather than forcing one mould — but on either reading it remains general wisdom, not a guarantee.
SiteAssessment: Site position: Proverbs 22:6 is a general principle about formation, not a promise that can be used to guarantee a child's future faith or to assign blame when a grown child departs. Parents should take its encouragement seriously and its guarantee language loosely.

Passage: No Evil Shall Befall Thee — the Protection Psalm
Difficulty: 'There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling. For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.' Readers who trust God and still suffer illness, bereavement, or violence ask the obvious question: was the promise false, or was their trust defective? The difficulty sharpens because the devil himself quotes verses 11-12 to Jesus in the wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:6), pressing the psalm as a guarantee that God must prevent even a stubbed foot.
Explanations: The psalm is poetic assurance, not a talisman or a contract. Its language is that of refuge and trust (verses 1-2, 9, 14): those who dwell in God's shelter are held in God's care, and the psalm's sweeping 'no evil' language expresses the security of that relationship in the absolute terms poetry uses, not a statistical claim that the faithful never suffer. Jesus' answer to the quotation is itself part of the resolution: to demand spectacular protection on cue is to test God rather than trust him (Matthew 4:7). The psalm's own ending promises deliverance and presence 'in trouble' (verse 15) — help within trouble, not exemption from it — which is why the psalm can be prayed honestly by sufferers rather than only by the untouched.
SiteAssessment: Site position: Psalm 91 promises God's keeping presence and ultimate deliverance, not immunity from harm in this life. Reading it as a guarantee that nothing bad will happen misuses the psalm in exactly the way the wilderness temptation models.

Passage: The Righteous Are Never Forsaken — or Begging Bread
Difficulty: 'I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.' Honest readers can point to righteous people who have gone hungry, lost everything, or depended on charity — including in Scripture itself. If this is a universal factual claim, it appears false; if it is a promise, it appears broken.
Explanations: The verse is the testimony of an aged observer within a wisdom psalm, not a doctrinal definition of how God treats every righteous person at every moment. Psalm 37 as a whole contrasts the temporary flourishing of the wicked with the lasting security of the righteous, and verse 25 states the psalmist's lifetime observation: as a pattern, God does not abandon his people to destitution, and his people's households are not left to beg as their settled condition. Temporary need, dependence on others' generosity, and seasons of real want are not what the verse denies; a final, forsaken end is. The verse is also framed as personal witness ('I have not seen'), which is weaker in form — and more honest — than a universal law.
SiteAssessment: Site position: Psalm 37:25 is observed wisdom about God's ordinary faithfulness to his people over a lifetime, not a promise that no righteous person will ever know want. It should comfort, not be used to shame the poor or to measure anyone's righteousness by their bank balance.

Passage: Why Do the Wicked Prosper? The Psalm That Answers Itself
Difficulty: The psalmist says plainly, 'I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked,' and 'these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches' — then, 'Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.' The question is whether the psalm endorses the complaint or resolves it.
Explanations: The psalm resolves its own tension, and that arc is the point. The complaint occupies the first half; the turn comes in verse 17, 'until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.' Seen from the end rather than the middle, the wicked's prosperity is slippery ground (verse 18) and the psalmist's nearness to God is itself the good (verse 28). The psalm does not deny the observed facts — the wicked do prosper for a time — nor does it claim the righteous never doubt. It relocates the question from present prosperity to final outcome and present communion: what matters is not who is richer now, but where each path ends and who walks with God meanwhile.

Difficulty: 'Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?' Taken alone, the verse sounds like advice to be only moderately good — as if excessive righteousness were dangerous and a little wickedness prudent. That reading collides with the rest of Scripture's call to wholehearted obedience, and with the book's own conclusion to fear God and keep his commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
Explanations: The verse is read in its immediate context (Ecclesiastes 7:15-18), where the Preacher has just observed that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness and the wicked prolong life in wickedness. 'Righteous overmuch' is therefore widely understood as over-scrupulous, self-righteous, or showy righteousness — a rigid moral performance that claims more wisdom and virtue than a human possesses and destroys the person practising it — paired with the matching warning in verse 17 not to be overmuch wicked either. The counsel is for balance against two kinds of extremism, not for a middle dose of sin: fear God (verse 18) rather than trusting one's own moral system to control outcomes. The verse warns against weaponised virtue, not against virtue itself.
SiteAssessment: Site position: Ecclesiastes 7:16 warns against self-righteous excess and the illusion that perfect performance controls life's outcomes. It is not permission to be half-hearted about obedience, and it must be read with verse 18's call to fear God, not with verse 16 alone.

Difficulty: If God is good, how can he say, 'I create evil'? The verse seems to make God the author of moral evil, which would contradict his goodness, his holiness, and passages that say God cannot be tempted by evil and tempts no one.

Difficulty: God says that if he threatens a nation with destruction and it repents, he will relent, and if he promises blessing and it does evil, he will change his purpose. If prophecy can be reversed, how can any prophecy be trusted, and does God change his mind?
Explanations: Jeremiah 18 states the principle itself: most prophetic announcements of judgment or blessing carry an implied condition, because their purpose is to move people to repentance or faithfulness. This does not make every prophecy conditional: unconditional promises, such as the promise of a new covenant and of a Davidic king, are stated without that condition and are not revoked by this principle. The test is in the text of each prophecy, not in a rule applied to all of them.

Difficulty: Jeremiah says, 'O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived.' If God deceived his own prophet, God would be a deceiver, and Jeremiah's complaint would accuse God of lying.
Explanations: The Hebrew verb can mean persuaded, enticed, or overpowered, and the verse itself glosses it: 'thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed.' Jeremiah is speaking in lament, the raw language of a man overwhelmed by a calling he did not seek and by the mockery it brought him. He is not making a doctrinal claim that God lied to him; in the same chapter he confesses God's presence with him and continues to preach. Lament uses extreme, emotional language to protest before God, and it must be read as complaint, not as a theological definition of God's character.

Passage: Jeremiah Curses the Day He Was Born
Difficulty: A faithful prophet curses the day of his birth and asks why he came from the womb only to see labour and sorrow. If even Jeremiah despairs like this, does faith fail, and is such cursing acceptable speech for a believer?
Explanations: This is lament, in the same tradition as Job's curse on his day of birth. Jeremiah does not curse God, deny God's existence, or abandon his calling; he protests the suffering his calling has brought him, in prayer, to God himself. Scripture preserves such laments precisely because despair and faith can coexist in the same person: the complaint is directed to God rather than away from him, and the book goes on with Jeremiah still speaking God's word.

Difficulty: Ezekiel 16 describes Jerusalem as an abandoned infant raised by God, then as an adulterous wife who pays her lovers, in graphic sexual detail. Readers ask whether such language is appropriate in Scripture, whether it demeans women, and whether God is pictured as an abusive husband.
Explanations: The chapter is an extended allegory of covenant unfaithfulness, not a literal account of a marriage and not an endorsement of its imagery as a model for human relationships. Jerusalem's 'lovers' are foreign gods and alliances; her 'adultery' is idolatry and political apostasy after extraordinary grace. Prophetic shock language is deliberate: it is meant to make comfortable idolatry feel as shocking as it is. The chapter ends not with rejection but with an everlasting covenant and atonement, which shows the allegory's point is restoration after judgment, not humiliation for its own sake.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The imagery is allegorical covenant language, shocking by design, and it must not be read literally or used to justify any human treatment of a spouse. Its endpoint is grace: God remembers his covenant and restores.

Difficulty: Ezekiel 23 names two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, and describes their sexual promiscuity in even more explicit terms than chapter 16. The passage is often skipped in public reading, and readers ask why Scripture contains pornographic detail at all.

Its graphic language serves a moral purpose — to expose idolatry as betrayal — and it should be taught with that allegorical key stated plainly, especially with younger readers.

Passage: The Soul That Sins Shall Die
Difficulty: 'The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' That seems to contradict passages where God visits the iniquity of fathers on children, and it raises the question whether children are punished for their parents' sins or whether each person stands alone.
Explanations: Ezekiel is addressing a legal and judicial question in Judah: people were using the proverb about sour grapes to claim they were being punished for their ancestors' sins rather than their own. God's answer concerns judicial guilt before him: a righteous son is not condemned for a wicked father's crimes, nor a wicked son acquitted by a righteous father. Other passages about consequences describe something different: the historical and family consequences of sin do fall on later generations, and God may judge a nation corporately, without making each individual judicially guilty for another's act.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: Individual judicial guilt is not inherited, while historical consequences of sin can still be inherited. Both statements are true in their own sphere, and neither should be used to cancel the other.

Difficulty: Ezekiel's opening vision — a whirlwind, four living creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, and a throne of sapphire — reads like a machine or a hallucination, and modern readers sometimes treat it as a literal vehicle or an ancient UFO account.
Explanations: The vision is a throne theophany, a symbolic picture of God's glory, mobility, and holiness, built from temple and royal imagery his exiled audience would recognise: cherubim, fire, wheels for movement in every direction, eyes for omniscience. Its details are symbolic, not engineering specifications: the wheels do not turn aside because God's purpose does not swerve, and the creatures' faces gather the highest forms of created life around the throne. Ezekiel himself falls on his face, which is the vision's intended response, not technical analysis.

Difficulty: God commands Ezekiel to bake his bread over human dung as a sign, then relents and allows cow dung instead. Readers ask why God would command something defiling, and whether the concession means God changed his mind about his own command.
Explanations: The act is a sign, not a diet: during a siege, food would be scarce and defiled, and Ezekiel's daily ration and defiled cooking dramatise that reality to an audience that would not listen to words. The concession matters: Ezekiel protests on grounds of ritual purity, and God grants cow dung, which was ordinary fuel, while keeping the sign's meaning. The passage shows a prophet's objection being heard within obedience, not a God who casually orders defilement and then reverses himself.

Difficulty: Daniel says Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem in the third year of Jehoiakim, but Jeremiah calls the fourth year of Jehoiakim the first year of Nebuchadnezzar. Both cannot be right about the same year, so one of the books appears to misdate the siege.
Explanations: The two books count regnal years differently, as ancient Near Eastern kingdoms did. Judah counted a king's accession year as his first year, while Babylon counted the accession year as year zero and the following year as year one. On Babylonian counting Daniel's 'third year' and on Judean counting Jeremiah's 'fourth year' describe the same period, around 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar first asserted control over Jerusalem after Carchemish. The difference is a dating convention, not a contradiction in the event.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The dates agree once each book's counting convention is recognised. This is a textual and calendrical resolution, not a choice between Daniel and Jeremiah.

Passage: Yet Forty Days, and Nineveh Shall Be Overthrown
Difficulty: Jonah proclaims without qualification, 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,' but Nineveh repents and God does not overthrow it. The prophecy appears to fail, which by the Deuteronomy test would mark Jonah as a false prophet.
Explanations: Prophetic warnings of judgment carry the implied condition stated in Jeremiah 18: if the threatened people turn, God relents. The warning's purpose is repentance, and Nineveh's repentance is the warning's success, not its failure. Jonah himself knows this: his flight and his later anger both assume God is merciful and will relent if Nineveh repents. The forty days are a deadline for repentance, and the city's fasting, including its king, is the response the warning was designed to produce.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The prophecy did not fail; it was a conditional warning, and it worked. A threat that produces repentance has achieved its purpose, and God's relenting is mercy, not inconsistency.

Difficulty: Jonah is angry that God spares Nineveh, argues with God about a plant, and wishes to die. The book ends with a question and no answer from Jonah. Readers ask why the story leaves its prophet unrepentant, and whether God is unfair to care about Israel's enemies.
Explanations: The book is a satirical prophetic critique, and Jonah is its foil, not its hero. His anger exposes a nationalism that wants God's mercy for Israel and God's judgment for Assyria, while God asks whether he should not pity a great city full of people who cannot discern right from left, and also much cattle. The plant that shades Jonah for a day and then withers is the argument in miniature: Jonah pities a plant he did not make, while begrudging God pity for a city he did make. The unanswered ending turns the question on the reader.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: God's mercy to repentant enemies is the book's point, and Jonah's anger is the error it exposes. The ending is deliberately open because the reader is meant to answer it.

Passage: Shall There Be Evil in a City?
Difficulty: Amos asks, 'shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?' Like Isaiah 45:7, the verse seems to attribute evil to God, which sits uneasily with God's goodness.
Explanations: The word is again ra', calamity or disaster, and the context is a series of cause-and-effect questions about disaster and warning: a trumpet sounds, the people tremble, a disaster falls, and the prophet asks whether it came without God's hand. Amos is claiming that national calamity is not random and not outside God's sovereignty, especially the judgment his book announces on Israel. He is not saying God commits the moral evil that brings the judgment.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The verse claims God's sovereignty over calamity and judgment, not authorship of sin. It should be read with Isaiah 45:7, where the same word carries the same sense.

Difficulty: God says, 'I hate, I despise your feast days,' and tells Israel to take away the noise of its songs. If God commanded feasts and sacrifices, how can he hate the very worship he ordered, and does this passage abolish ritual worship?
Explanations: The hatred is directed at worship divorced from justice, not at worship itself. The surrounding verses name the problem: the same people who keep feasts oppress the poor, take bribes, and turn justice to wormwood. God rejects offerings brought by hands still doing injustice, and calls instead for justice to roll down like waters. The passage does not cancel the sacrificial system; it insists that ritual without righteousness is hypocrisy, a theme the prophets repeat and Jesus repeats.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: God rejects hypocritical worship, not worship. The passage condemns feasts offered alongside oppression; it does not teach that God never wanted sacrifice or song.

Difficulty: Obadiah says of the house of Esau that 'there shall not be any remaining.' Yet Edomites appear later in history, most famously Herod, an Idumean. The prophecy of total extinction appears to have failed.
Explanations: Prophetic judgment language uses totalising, hyperbolic terms for the fall of a nation as a political power, not as a census claim that no individual of that ancestry will ever live again. Edom as a kingdom was destroyed, its territory taken, and its people absorbed and displaced, which is what the oracle announces: the house of Jacob as fire consuming the house of Esau as stubble. Later individuals of Edomite descent, living under other powers centuries later, do not revive Edom as the nation Obadiah judged. The same hyperbolic idiom is used for other nations in the prophets.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The prophecy announces Edom's end as a nation and power, in the hyperbolic language of judgment oracles. Later Edomite individuals do not contradict that national judgment.

Difficulty: Nahum ends with all who hear of Nineveh's fall clapping their hands over her, because her wickedness passed continually over everyone. After Jonah, where God spares repentant Nineveh, Nahum seems to celebrate its destruction, and readers ask whether rejoicing over an enemy's ruin is compatible with mercy.
Explanations: The two books concern different generations, about a century and a half apart. Jonah's Nineveh repented and was spared; Nahum's Nineveh returned to the cruelty, plunder, and treachery the book documents, and after further warning it fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC. Nahum's 'clapping' is the relief of oppressed peoples at the end of an empire that had terrorised them continually, not a command to gloat over personal enemies. The book's opening also insists God is slow to anger and a stronghold to those who trust him.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The celebration is relief at justice after prolonged cruelty, in a later generation than Jonah's repentant city. Mercy was offered and refused over time; judgment, when it came, ended an oppressor, and the victims' relief is understandable without making cruelty a virtue.

Difficulty: Lamentations says God 'doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men,' yet asks, 'Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?' If God afflicts Jerusalem, how can he not afflict willingly, and does evil proceed from God?
Explanations: The two verses describe two different things. Verse 33 says affliction is not God's delight or first desire: he does not enjoy grief for its own sake. Verse 38, in the form of a rhetorical question, acknowledges that both good and calamity come under God's sovereign ordering — again, ra' as calamity, not moral evil. The chapter holds them together: Jerusalem's suffering is real, God is sovereign over it, and it is not what God delights in. The sufferer's response in the chapter is to hope in God's mercies, which are new every morning.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: God can sovereignly permit and ordain calamity in judgment without delighting in affliction. The passage distinguishes God's delight from God's sovereignty, and that distinction resolves the apparent contradiction.

Passage: I Will Utterly Consume All Things
Difficulty: Zephaniah opens with God saying he will 'utterly consume all things from off the land,' including man, beast, birds, and fish. The universal scope seems to contradict the same book's promise of a remnant, and the literal extinction of all life never happened.
Explanations: Prophetic judgment opens with sweeping, cosmic language to convey total judgment on Judah, then narrows to specific targets: idolaters, complacent officials, and violent households in Jerusalem. The 'all things' language is hyperbolic scope-setting, a reversal of creation order that signals the seriousness of the Day of the LORD, not a literal prediction that every animal on earth would die in Judah's judgment. The book itself then preserves a remnant — the humble who seek righteousness — which shows the universal opening was never meant as an unqualified census of survivors.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The opening is hyperbolic judgment language for total judgment on Judah, followed in the same book by a remnant. Reading the first verses as literal global extinction ignores the book's own narrowing and its remnant promise.

Difficulty: Malachi says Israel has robbed God in tithes and offerings and invites them, 'prove me now herewith,' promising blessing until there is not room enough to receive it. Readers ask whether this is a general promise that generous giving guarantees material prosperity, and whether testing God is even allowed.
Explanations: The passage is addressed to covenant Israel under the Mosaic system, where tithes supported the Levites and the temple storehouse, and withholding them was covenant theft, not merely stinginess. The invitation to 'prove' God is a specific covenant challenge in that setting, tied to the land's agricultural blessing, not a universal formula that any gift purchases wealth. The New Testament's giving pattern is cheerful, generous, and sacrificial, but it never repeats Malachi's storehouse promise as a prosperity guarantee.
SiteAssessment: Site assessment: The passage concerns Israel's covenant tithes and temple support, not a prosperity formula for all believers. Generosity is commanded, but Malachi 3 does not promise that giving buys material wealth.

Passage: The Wording of the Sign over the Cross
Difficulty: The four Gospels do not give the sign over Jesus' head in identical words. Matthew has 'THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS', Mark has only 'THE KING OF THE JEWS', Luke has 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS', and John has 'JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS'. If the sign said one thing, why do the accounts disagree? A reader who expects a verbatim transcript sees four different inscriptions and wonders whether any of them can be trusted.
Explanations: The main explanation is that no Gospel claims to reproduce the sign word for word. John notes the sign was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so any single wording in Greek already involves selection and translation from a three-language notice, and each writer quotes the part that serves his account: Matthew keeps the name and the charge, Mark shortens to the charge alone, Luke and John keep fuller forms. A second, compatible point is abbreviation: ancient writers regularly shortened inscriptions and speeches rather than inventing them, and the core charge — that Jesus was executed as 'King of the Jews' — is identical in all four. A minority worry remains only if verbatim reporting is demanded of texts that never promise it.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the differences are differences of selection and abbreviation, not competing facts about what the charge was. All four agree on the substance, and the variation is exactly what independent reports of a three-language public notice would produce. This entry does not claim Scripture itself settles the point in these words; that is the site's reading of the evidence.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Centurion's Servant: Who Came to Jesus?
Difficulty: Matthew says the centurion himself came to Jesus and spoke to him, while Luke says the centurion stayed at home and sent Jewish elders, then friends, to speak on his behalf. Both cannot be literally true in the same sense: either the man came in person or he did not. Readers ask whether one writer has simply got the scene wrong.
Explanations: The widely accepted explanation is ancient agency: in the ancient world, and in ordinary language still, a person is said to do what he does through his authorised messengers. Matthew compresses the messengers out and reports the centurion as the actor; Luke spells out the intermediaries. Luke's own version supports this, since the friends carry the centurion's words in the first person ('I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof'), showing the message counted as his speech. There is no disagreement about the request, the faith Jesus commends, or the healing at a distance.
SiteAssessment: Site position — this is compression, not contradiction. Matthew reports the action, Luke reports the means, and both describe the same encounter. The site does not present this as Scripture's own verdict; it is the site's assessment of how the two accounts fit.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 8; Luke 7); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: One Blind Man or Two at Jericho?
Difficulty: Matthew says two blind men were healed as Jesus left Jericho; Mark names one, blind Bartimaeus, as Jesus left Jericho; Luke says one blind man was healed as Jesus approached Jericho. The number differs, and so does the direction: approaching versus leaving. A reader wonders whether these are two different healings, or whether the writers disagree about a single one.
Explanations: On the number, the standard explanation is partial reporting: Matthew names both men, while Mark and Luke concentrate on one — Mark even names him, Bartimaeus, suggesting he was the better-known or more vocal of the two, the one who did the shouting. Mentioning one man does not deny a second. On the timing, two explanations are offered and are compatible: Jericho had an old site and a newer Herodian town, so a journey could leave one and approach the other; or Luke groups the healing with the approach while Matthew and Mark place it at the departure, the healing belonging to the same pass through the town. The core — blind men calling on Jesus as Son of David, healed at Jericho — is common to all three.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the one-versus-two difference is settled by partial reporting and is not a contradiction. The approaching-versus-leaving detail is less certain, and the site does not force it: the two-Jerichos explanation is plausible but not provable from the texts alone. That uncertainty is stated, not hidden.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 20; Mark 10; Luke 18); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Anointings of Jesus: One Event or Several?
Difficulty: Four anointing scenes look similar and different at once: a woman anoints Jesus with costly ointment, someone objects to the waste, Jesus defends her. But the settings differ — Simon the leper's house in Bethany near the Passion, a Pharisee's house early in the ministry, Lazarus's household six days before Passover — and the details differ too: head or feet, hair or not, a named Mary or an unnamed 'sinner'. Readers ask whether the writers have confused one event, or whether Jesus was anointed three times.
Explanations: The consensus reading is two events, not one and not three. Matthew, Mark, and John describe the same Bethany anointing near the end: same town, same objection about selling the ointment for the poor, same defence pointing to burial. Their differences are complementary — Matthew and Mark mention the head, John mentions the feet and names Mary, and a single anointing can involve both. Luke's scene is the distinct one: it happens early, in a Pharisee's house, with an unnamed woman known as a sinner, and its point is forgiveness, not burial. Treating Luke's scene as the same event would require moving it years and changing its host, its woman, and its meaning.
SiteAssessment: Site position — two anointings, one in Luke's early ministry and one at Bethany in Passion week, best fits all four texts. The site does not claim certainty about every detail of the Bethany scene, but the case for separating Luke's account is strong, and conflating all four into one event does more violence to the texts than keeping two.

Difficulty: Mark 16:9-20, with its appearances, commission, and signs such as handling serpents and drinking poison, reads like a fitting ending. But it is absent from the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts, and early church writers show knowledge of Mark ending at 16:8, with the women fleeing the tomb in fear. Readers ask: is this passage Scripture, was it added later, and can anything built on it — especially the signs in verses 17-18 — be trusted?
Explanations: Textual scholars widely agree the long ending was not part of Mark's original text: it is missing from the two earliest complete Greek Bibles, its vocabulary and style differ from the rest of Mark, and it reads like a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts. What is debated is what Mark originally intended: whether his Gospel was meant to end abruptly at 16:8, with fear and silence as a deliberate, unsettling close, or whether an original ending was lost very early and 16:9-20 was supplied to fill the gap. No core Christian doctrine depends on these verses — the resurrection appearances and the commission are fully attested elsewhere — and the signs in verses 17-18 were never a general command to test God with poison or snakes.
SiteAssessment: Site position — Mark 16:9-20 should be read as a later addition, honestly marked as such, not as Mark's own ending. Readers should not build doctrine or practice on verses 17-18 alone, and the abrupt ending at 16:8 should be allowed to stand as the text Mark's earliest readers received. This is the site's textual judgment, not a claim that Scripture itself labels the passage.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Mark 16); standard manuscript summaries (early Greek witnesses omit Mark 16:9-20); no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: The story of the woman taken in adultery — 'he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her' and 'neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more' — is one of the best-loved passages in the Gospels. But it is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John, it floats in different places in later copies, and some manuscripts omit it entirely. Readers ask whether a beloved story can be genuine if it was not in John's original Gospel, and whether 'neither do I condemn thee' softens Jesus' teaching on sin.
Explanations: Textual scholars widely agree the passage was not part of John's original text: it is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts and early writers do not cite it as part of John, and its style fits Luke better than John, which is why some later copies place it after Luke 21. Many scholars still regard it as an ancient, possibly authentic tradition about Jesus that circulated independently before being inserted into John, because it coheres with his mercy toward sinners and his refusal to be used as a trap. The passage itself does not excuse the sin: Jesus both refuses condemnation by the crowd and commands 'sin no more'.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the passage should be read with its textual history stated openly: almost certainly not John's own composition, but an early tradition consistent with Jesus as the Gospels portray him. It should not be used to argue that Jesus was indifferent to sexual sin, nor removed from devotional reading; honesty about its status and about its final command belong together.
