Difficulty: Jesus says, 'If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.' Taken literally, this seems to command hatred of family and even of oneself, contradicting the command to honour parents and love one's neighbour. Readers wonder whether discipleship really requires hating the people they are also commanded to love.
Explanations: The widely accepted explanation is Semitic idiom: in biblical language 'hate' often means 'love less' or 'put second' by comparison, not emotional hatred. Matthew's parallel makes the meaning explicit: 'He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me' (Matthew 10:37). The context confirms it: Luke 14 is about counting the cost of following Jesus, and the point is that loyalty to Jesus must outrank even the strongest family loyalty when the two conflict. Jesus elsewhere upholds honouring parents and caring for family, so a literal hatred reading would make him contradict himself within the same teaching ministry.
SiteAssessment: Site position — 'hate' here is comparative, not a command to feel hatred. Discipleship may cost family approval, and sometimes family closeness, but it never licenses contempt for parents or neglect of family duty. That is the site's reading of the idiom and the parallel text, not a verdict Scripture pronounces on itself.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Luke 14; Matthew 10); general background on Semitic comparative idiom; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: A Gentile woman begs Jesus to heal her demon-possessed daughter. Jesus first says nothing, then says he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, then says, 'It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it to dogs.' To modern ears this sounds like an ethnic insult and a refusal, from a man who elsewhere welcomes outsiders. Readers ask whether Jesus was being cruel, whether he shared the prejudices of his day, or whether he changed his mind.
Explanations: The context points away from a final refusal and toward a testing of faith that ends in commendation. The word for 'dogs' here is the diminutive used for household dogs, not the street scavengers of common insult, and the woman answers within the image — even the dogs eat the crumbs — rather than protesting it. Jesus then praises her: 'O woman, great is thy faith,' and heals her daughter at once. Two readings of the testing are offered: that Jesus is drawing out her persistence so the disciples, who wanted her sent away, can see Gentile faith; or that he is voicing, to expose and then overturn, the exclusive attitude around him. On either reading, the passage ends with inclusion, not rejection, and it stands beside other Gentile welcomes in both Gospels.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the passage is not evidence that Jesus despised Gentiles, and it should not be softened into pretending the words are not sharp. The sharpness is real, the testing is purposeful, and the outcome — public praise and immediate healing — is the passage's verdict on her faith. The site holds the testing reading while acknowledging that the exact tone of Jesus' words cannot be recovered with certainty.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 15; Mark 7); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Cursing of the Fig Tree
Difficulty: Jesus, hungry, finds a fig tree in leaf but with no fruit, curses it, and it withers. Readers stumble twice: it seems petty and destructive to kill a tree for being out of season — Mark even notes 'the time of figs was not yet' — and it seems unlike Jesus, who elsewhere feeds crowds and heals, to use power to destroy. Is this a loss of temper, or does the tree mean something more?
Explanations: The widely accepted reading is that this is an acted parable, not a botanical complaint. A fig tree in leaf advertised fruit; finding leaves without figs pictured Israel's temple system — impressive foliage, no fruit — and Mark places the cursing around the temple cleansing, sandwiching the two scenes so each interprets the other. Matthew compresses the timeline, as he often does, so the withering looks immediate. The point is judgment on fruitlessness, not anger at a tree: the tree stands for a people and an institution that bore the appearance of godliness without its fruit. The passage is therefore about the temple's coming judgment, and secondarily about prayer and faith, which both accounts attach to it.
SiteAssessment: Site position — read as an acted parable of judgment, the passage is coherent and serious, not a tantrum. The site does not claim this removes all discomfort: a sign-act of judgment is still a judgment, and readers who feel its severity are feeling what the passage intends. What it does not support is reading the tree as a mere victim of bad temper.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 21; Mark 11); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Gerasene Demoniac and the Drowning of the Pigs
Difficulty: Jesus casts demons out of a man (or two men) into a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the sea and drown. Readers stumble on several fronts at once: the number of men differs between Matthew and Mark/Luke, the place-name differs (Gergesenes in Matthew's KJV, Gadarenes in Mark's), and the destruction of a large herd — someone's livelihood — seems a disproportionate price for one healing, and cruel to animals.
Explanations: On the number and place, the same partial-reporting and regional explanations apply as at Jericho: Matthew mentions two demoniacs, Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent one, and Gadara, Gerasa, and Gergesa were towns of the same lakeside region, so writers could name the district differently without disagreeing about the shore. On the pigs, the context matters: this is Gentile territory, the pigs are unclean animals, and the man's deliverance — a human being restored to his right mind, clothed, and sent home to tell his story — is presented as worth more than the herd. The loss also exposes the townspeople's values: they beg Jesus to leave rather than welcome the healed man. The passage does not present animal suffering as unimportant, but it ranks a person's liberation above property, and it does not make pig-drowning a general model for dealing with animals or livelihoods.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the differing numbers and place-names are regional and selective reporting, not contradictions, and the moral weight of the passage falls on the delivered man, not on the herd as a price Jesus was careless about. The site acknowledges the economic loss was real and the townspeople's dismay understandable; the passage's point is that they valued the herd over the man, and invites readers to notice which they value.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 8; Mark 5; Luke 8); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Two Thieves on the Cross
Difficulty: Matthew says both criminals crucified with Jesus 'cast the same in his teeth' — both mocked him. Luke says one mocked him while the other rebuked the mocker, confessed his own guilt, asked Jesus to remember him, and heard, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.' Readers ask whether the second criminal changed sides, or whether one Gospel has rewritten the scene.
Explanations: The standard explanation is sequence: both men mocked Jesus at first, as Matthew summarises, and one of them then changed — convicted by Jesus' bearing, by his prayer for his executioners, or by the darkness and the conduct of the scene — and turned to him in repentance. Luke, who gives the fuller scene, reports the end of that arc rather than its beginning. Nothing in Luke denies an earlier mockery, and nothing in Matthew denies a later change of heart; each writer selects the phase that serves his account, Matthew the shared shame of the crucifixion, Luke the mercy extended even there.
SiteAssessment: Site position — a change of heart during the crucifixion best fits both texts, and the passage should be read as a story of last-minute repentance, not as a contradiction to be resolved by deleting either detail. The site does not claim to know what changed the man's mind; that the texts show a changed man is enough.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 27; Luke 23); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Cock Crow Once or Twice?
Difficulty: Jesus predicts Peter's denial with a detail that differs by Gospel: Matthew, Luke, and John say Peter will deny him before the cock crows, while Mark says before the cock crows twice. If Mark is right, the other three have the prediction wrong; if they are right, Mark has added a crow. Small as it seems, readers cite it as a clean, checkable contradiction.
Explanations: The explanation is counting, not error. Mark, the fullest account, counts both cock-crows of the night — the first, around midnight, and the second, toward dawn — and says Peter will deny Jesus three times before the second. The other writers mention only the final, decisive crow, the one that triggers Peter's remembering. Mark's own narrative fits this: Peter denies, a first crow sounds, and the denials continue until the second crow, when Peter weeps. No Gospel claims there was only one crow, and Mark does not claim the denials all happened before the first.
SiteAssessment: Site position — this is a difference of counting, resolved by Mark's fuller report. It is a useful test case: a seeming contradiction that dissolves once the accounts are read together rather than as competing transcripts.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 13); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: The risen Jesus says to Mary Magdalene, 'Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father.' Yet Matthew says the women 'held him by the feet, and worshipped him,' and a week later Jesus invites Thomas to touch his wounds. Readers ask whether Jesus contradicted himself, whether touching was forbidden on Sunday and allowed later, or whether the translation misleads.
Explanations: The widely accepted resolution is translation: the Greek verb with its present imperative is better rendered 'stop clinging to me' or 'do not hold on to me' than a blanket ban on touching. Mary, weeping and overwhelmed, was clinging to Jesus as if the old companionship could simply resume; Jesus redirects her to the new situation — he is ascending, and she must go and tell his brethren. That fits Matthew, where holding his feet in worship is not rebuked, and Thomas, where touching is invited as evidence. The difference is between clinging to prevent departure and touching in worship or belief, not between two rules about contact.
SiteAssessment: Site position — 'do not cling to me' is the better reading, and it removes the apparent contradiction with Matthew 28:9 and John 20:27. The site notes this is a translation judgment, widely shared but not unanimous in wording, and the underlying point — that resurrection changes the mode of Jesus' presence — stands on either rendering.
Sources: On-site KJV text (John 20; Matthew 28); general background on the Greek present imperative; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: Jesus says, 'My Father is greater than I.' Readers who hold that Jesus is fully God ask how the Father can be greater if Father and Son are equal; readers who deny his divinity cite the verse as proof that Jesus himself disclaimed equality. The verse is a favourite proof-text on both sides, which is itself a sign that it needs careful reading.
Explanations: The orthodox reading, held across the early creeds and the mainstream traditions, is that 'greater' refers to role and position in the work of redemption, not to essence or being. The Son, in becoming man and in going to the Father, stands in the position of one sent and obedient; the Father, as sender, is greater in that order of mission. John himself supplies the balancing texts: 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30) and the Word 'was God' (John 1:1), so John cannot mean by 14:28 that the Son is a lesser being without contradicting his own Gospel. Non-trinitarian readings take 'greater' as ontological, but that requires setting aside those balancing passages.
SiteAssessment: Site position — 'greater' denotes the Son's incarnate mission and order, not a lesser divinity. This is the site's doctrinal position, stated as such: the verse is not, on its own, a denial of Christ's deity, and it should be read with John's whole portrait of Jesus, not as an isolated slogan.
Sources: On-site KJV text (John 14; John 1; John 10); general doctrinal summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Son Not Knowing the Day or Hour
Difficulty: Jesus says of the day and hour of his return, 'knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.' If Jesus is omniscient God, how can he not know something? If he genuinely did not know, how can he be God? Readers also note that some manuscripts omit 'neither the Son' from Matthew's version, and ask whether the harder reading was softened by copyists.
Explanations: The mainstream orthodox explanation distinguishes the Son's two natures: as God, the Son shares the Father's knowledge; as man, in the state of humiliation, he genuinely lived within human limitations, including not knowing — or at least not revealing — the day and hour. The point of the saying in context is pastoral, not speculative: no one can calculate the end, so watchfulness, not date-setting, is required. Textually, Mark's version retains 'neither the Son' in the earliest witnesses, and Matthew's omission in some copies looks like scribal softening of a hard saying, which if anything confirms the saying's authenticity — copyists tend to remove difficulties, not invent them.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the saying is best understood as the incarnate Son speaking within his genuine human limitation, without surrendering his deity. The site does not pretend the mechanics of two-natures knowledge are fully explicable; it holds that the passage teaches human limitation in the incarnation and forbids date-setting, and that is enough to remove the supposed contradiction with Christ's divinity.
RelatedTopics: Second Coming; Son of God; Christology; Eschatology
Sources: On-site KJV text (Mark 13; Matthew 24); standard manuscript summaries (Mark 13:32 retains 'neither the Son'); no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: 'I Came Not to Send Peace, but a Sword'
Difficulty: Jesus says, 'Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.' This sounds like a call to violence from the Prince of Peace, and it sits uneasily beside 'blessed are the peacemakers' and his rebuke of Peter's sword in Gethsemane. Readers ask whether Jesus endorsed armed conflict, or family strife.
Explanations: The context and Luke's parallel settle the image: Luke has 'division' where Matthew has 'sword', and Matthew immediately explains the sword as division within households — father against son, mother against daughter — when family members take different sides over Jesus. The sword is metaphorical, for the cutting effect of allegiance, not a weapon to be taken up: the same Jesus forbids his disciples to fight for him at his arrest and teaches love of enemies. The passage is therefore about cost, not combat: following Jesus can divide even families, and disciples must be prepared for that division without creating it by violence or cruelty.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the sword is division over allegiance, not a licence for violence. Any use of this verse to justify coercion or family cruelty misreads it, and the site states that plainly as its own reading.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 10; Luke 12); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: The Rich Young Ruler and the Camel's Needle
Difficulty: A rich young ruler asks what good thing he must do for eternal life, keeps the commandments from his youth, and is told to sell all he has, give to the poor, and follow Jesus — and he goes away sorrowful. Jesus then says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, and the disciples ask, 'Who then can be saved?' Readers ask whether wealth itself damns, whether every Christian must sell everything, and whether salvation is by works after all.
Explanations: The passage's own answer is grace, not a wealth ban and not works: 'With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.' The camel and the needle are deliberate hyperbole for impossibility, and the ruler's problem is not the size of his bank balance but the one thing he will not surrender — the idol that keeps him from following. The command to sell all is addressed to this man, exposing his specific attachment, not issued as a universal rule: other wealthy followers, such as Joseph of Arimathaea, are not told to do the same, and the early church's sharing was voluntary. The disciples' alarm is the point: if even a moral, wealthy, law-keeping man cannot save himself, no one can — salvation must be God's work.
SiteAssessment: Site position — wealth is a danger because it can become the thing a person will not surrender, not a sin in itself, and the passage teaches impossibility for man and possibility with God. The site does not read 'sell all' as a standing order to every believer, and it does not soften the warning either: whatever a person will not give up for Christ is functioning as their god.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Luke 18); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: The rich young ruler addresses Jesus as 'Good Master', and Jesus replies, 'Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God.' Readers who believe Jesus is God ask why he would deflect a true title; readers who deny his divinity cite the verse as Jesus' own denial that he is good, and therefore that he is God.
Explanations: The saying is best read as a question, not a denial. Jesus takes the man's word 'good' seriously and presses it: do you realise what you are saying? If only God is good, then calling Jesus good either means recognising who he is, or using a flattering title without understanding it. The context supports this: Jesus does not say 'I am not good,' he asks why the title is given, and then goes on to claim the authority to set the terms of eternal life and discipleship. Matthew's version, 'Why callest thou me good?' followed by 'if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments,' keeps the same probing tone. Read as a denial, the verse would contradict the Gospels' portrait of a sinless Jesus; read as a probe, it invites the ruler — and the reader — to follow the title to its conclusion.
SiteAssessment: Site position — Jesus is probing the title, not disowning it. The site holds that reading because it fits the immediate context and the Gospels as a whole, while acknowledging that the verse, taken alone, can be made to sound like a denial — which is why it must not be taken alone.
RelatedTopics: Son of God; Christology; Biblical Interpretation
Sources: On-site KJV text (Mark 10; Luke 18; Matthew 19); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: Why Was the Sinless Jesus Baptised?
Difficulty: John's baptism was a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Jesus, whom the Gospels present as sinless, comes to be baptised by John, and John himself objects: 'I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?' Readers ask why a sinless man would submit to a rite for sinners, and whether this implies Jesus had sins to confess.
Explanations: Jesus' own answer is the key: 'Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.' The baptism is not a confession of personal sin but an identification — Jesus stands with the people he came to save, submits to God's appointed way, and is publicly marked out at the start of his ministry, with the Spirit descending and the Father's voice affirming him. John consents on that basis. The Gospels never suggest Jesus confessed sins at the Jordan; the rite's meaning changes because the person undergoing it changes it, from repentance for one's own sins to solidarity with sinners and obedience to the Father.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the baptism is identification and obedience, not repentance for personal sin. The site states this as its reading of Jesus' own explanation, 'to fulfil all righteousness', read with the voice from heaven that follows it.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 3; Mark 1; Luke 3); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: Paul's conversion is told three times in Acts, and the details do not line up at first glance. In chapter 9 the men with Paul 'stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man'; in chapter 22 they 'saw indeed the light' but 'heard not the voice of him that spake to me'; in chapter 26 Paul says 'we were all fallen to the earth'. Did they stand or fall, hear or not hear, see or not see? Readers ask whether Luke contradicts himself within one book.
Explanations: The differences are largely ones of perspective and sequence, and the Greek verb for hearing helps with the main one: it can mean hearing a sound and it can mean understanding words, so the companions can have heard a sound without hearing — that is, understanding — the voice that spoke to Paul. Similarly, they can have fallen to the ground at the light and then stood speechless afterward; chapter 9 describes them standing in bewilderment, chapter 26 describes the initial fall. Each retelling is also shaped for its audience — a plain narrative in chapter 9, a defence before a Jerusalem crowd in chapter 22, a defence before Agrippa in chapter 26 — so Paul emphasises different details each time. The core is identical in all three: a blinding light, the risen Jesus speaking, Paul's commission to the Gentiles.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the three accounts are complementary retellings, not competing versions, and the hearing distinction and the fall-then-stand sequence resolve the apparent contradictions. The site notes the hearing explanation depends on the range of the Greek verb, which is real but should not be overstated as proof; the agreement on the core event is the stronger point.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Acts 9; Acts 22; Acts 26); general background on the Greek verb for hearing; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: From the cross Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.' It is one of the most quoted sayings of the crucifixion. But the saying is absent from some early manuscripts of Luke, and readers ask whether words they love were actually spoken, and whether their absence undermines the Gospels.
Explanations: Textual scholars note the saying is missing from several early witnesses, though it is present in many others and was known very early, and it is widely retained in modern editions, often with a note. Its absence in some copies is usually explained by scribal omission or by the difficulty of the saying itself — forgiving executioners is a hard word, and copyists sometimes remove hard words — rather than by late invention, since the sentiment matches Jesus' teaching on forgiving enemies and Stephen's parallel prayer in Acts 7. Unlike the long ending of Mark or the adultery passage, no doctrine hangs on this verse alone: Jesus' forgiveness of enemies is taught throughout the Gospels whether or not this sentence is original to Luke.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the saying should be retained in reading with its textual uncertainty noted, not presented as certain or suppressed as spurious. The site's judgment is that its early attestation and coherence with Jesus' teaching make retention reasonable, while honesty requires admitting some early copies lack it.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Luke 23; Acts 7); standard manuscript summaries (some early witnesses omit Luke 23:34a); no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: Two Animals at the Triumphal Entry?
Difficulty: Matthew says the disciples brought both an ass and a colt for the triumphal entry, and Jesus sat on them; Mark and Luke mention only a colt. Readers picture an absurd scene — Jesus riding two animals at once — and ask whether Matthew has misunderstood his own proof-text, Zechariah 9:9, which speaks of a king 'riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass'.
Explanations: Zechariah's lines are Hebrew poetic parallelism: the second line restates the first, describing one animal in two ways, not two animals. Matthew, writing for readers steeped in Scripture, treats the parallelism literally and brings both animals into the scene, with Jesus sitting on the clothes laid over them. Mark and Luke, writing more simply, report the colt that was actually ridden. The entry itself — a colt, garments spread, crowds crying Hosanna — is common to all three, and the difference is Matthew's scriptural style, not a competing memory of the procession. No Gospel claims Jesus straddled two animals simultaneously; the clothes, not a double saddle, are what he sat upon.
SiteAssessment: Site position — Matthew's two animals are a literalistic reading of Zechariah's parallelism, and the colt is the animal ridden. The site does not hide that Matthew's handling of the poetry looks odd to modern readers; it explains it as first-century scriptural method, not as evidence that the entry did not happen.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 21; Mark 11; Luke 19); general background on Hebrew parallelism in Zechariah 9:9; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: Two Birth Stories: Matthew and Luke
Difficulty: Matthew and Luke tell the birth of Jesus very differently. Matthew has wise men, a star, Herod's plot, and a flight into Egypt; Luke has a census, shepherds, a manger, and a presentation in the temple. Matthew's family seems to live in Bethlehem and then settle in Nazareth after Egypt; Luke's family travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem and returns to Nazareth. Readers ask whether these are two incompatible birth stories stitched together, or one story told from two sides.
Explanations: The accounts are complementary selections, not competing timelines. Matthew follows Joseph's perspective — his dream, his dilemma, his flight — and selects episodes that show Jesus as the threatened king and the new Moses who, like Israel, comes out of Egypt. Luke follows Mary's perspective, with the annunciation, the songs, and the shepherds, and selects episodes that show Jesus as Saviour for the lowly and the nations. Neither writer claims to give every episode: Matthew omits the census and shepherds, Luke omits the wise men and Egypt, and the two sets of episodes can be arranged in sequence (birth, shepherds, presentation, wise men, flight) without forcing either text. The shared core — virgin conception, birth in Bethlehem in David's line, naming by divine direction — is identical.
SiteAssessment: Site position — the birth narratives are complementary, not contradictory, and the differences of selection reflect the writers' different emphases, Joseph and kingship in Matthew, Mary and lowliness in Luke. The site does not claim every chronological join between the two is provable; it claims the accounts do not contradict each other on any point either writer actually asserts.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 1-2; Luke 1-2); general Gospel-background summaries; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Difficulty: Jesus says, 'As Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.' But the Gospels place the burial on Friday afternoon and the empty tomb on Sunday morning — barely a day and a half by modern counting, and only two nights. Readers ask whether Jesus' own prediction fails, or whether the church's Friday crucifixion is wrong.
Explanations: The widely accepted explanation is inclusive reckoning: in Jewish usage of the time, any part of a day counted as a day and a night, so Friday afternoon, Saturday, and Sunday morning count as three days. The Gospels themselves use 'after three days' and 'on the third day' interchangeably for the same interval, which confirms they are not counting seventy-two hours. The Jonah comparison is also typological rather than stopwatch-precise: as Jonah emerged from the fish, so Jesus emerges from the grave, with 'three days' as the conventional expression for a short, complete period. Alternative proposals — a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion — exist, but they create more problems with the Passover chronology than they solve, and they are not needed if inclusive counting is allowed.
SiteAssessment: Site position — inclusive day-counting resolves the difficulty, and 'on the third day' is how the Gospels themselves count it. The site does not present a Wednesday crucifixion as a live option for its readers; it is noted here only to show it was considered and set aside.
Sources: On-site KJV text (Matthew 12; Matthew 27-28); general background on Jewish inclusive day-reckoning; no copyrighted apologetics work consulted or copied.

Passage: Christ Became a Curse for Us
Difficulty: Paul says Christ was 'made a curse for us,' yet Deuteronomy says 'cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.' Readers stumble on whether this means Christ himself became cursed, evil, or rejected by God in his own person.
Explanations: The widely held reading is substitutionary: Christ bore the curse that the law pronounces on law-breakers, without himself becoming morally corrupt or ceasing to be the beloved Son. 'Curse' here names the penalty and the shame of crucifixion, not a change in Christ's character. Some readers press the wording further, but the mainstream explanation keeps the distinction between bearing a curse and being cursed in oneself.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Galatians 3:13 teaches penal substitution in this limited sense: Christ took the law's curse in our place on the cross. It does not teach that the Son became sinful or that the Father stopped loving him.
Sources: KJV text on site; standard reading of Deuteronomy 21:23 as cited by Paul; no specific modern work relied on.

Passage: Hagar and Sarah as an Allegory
Difficulty: Paul calls the story of Hagar and Sarah 'an allegory' and maps the two women onto two covenants. Readers worry this means Paul denied that Hagar and Sarah were real people, or that any Old Testament story may be turned into whatever meaning a reader prefers.
Explanations: The agreed reading is that Paul uses the historical story illustratively: he does not deny the events, he draws a comparison from them, as he says himself by naming Sinai and the Jerusalem above. Allegory here is Paul's own labelled illustration, not a licence for readers to allegorise every narrative at will. The historical account in Genesis and the covenant comparison in Galatians stand together.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Paul is illustrating from real history, not replacing it. Readers should not take this passage as permission to treat historical narratives as mere symbols.
Sources: KJV text on site; Paul's own framing in Galatians 4:24; Genesis account treated as history.

Passage: Made to Be Sin for Us
Difficulty: Paul says God 'hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin.' Taken literally, this seems to say Christ became sinful, which clashes with the same verse's claim that he knew no sin and with the rest of the New Testament's picture of a sinless Saviour.
Explanations: The standard explanation is that 'sin' here stands for a sin offering, as the Hebrew word for sin is used in Leviticus, or for Christ being treated as sin's bearer in our place. Either way the point is imputation, not corruption: our sin was reckoned to him and his righteousness to us. The verse's own contrast, between his knowing no sin and our becoming God's righteousness, points against a literal reading.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 2 Corinthians 5:21 teaches exchange, not transformation of Christ's character: he bore sin's penalty as our representative while remaining sinless.
Sources: KJV text on site; Levitical use of sin as sin offering; standard cross-reference to Isaiah 53.

Difficulty: Paul tells readers to 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,' which sounds like earning salvation by effort, especially when set beside his own teaching that salvation is by grace through faith and not of works.
Explanations: The context resolves the tension: verse 13 immediately adds that it is God who works in believers both to will and to do. 'Work out' means live out, carry to completion, what God has already given, not work for a salvation not yet possessed. Fear and trembling here describe serious, reverent obedience, not terror that God may drop the believer.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Philippians 2:12-13 teaches responsible obedience empowered by God, not self-earned salvation. The two verses must be read together, never verse 12 alone.
Sources: KJV text on site; immediate context of Philippians 2:13; comparison with Ephesians 2:8-10.

Difficulty: Christ is called 'the firstborn of every creature,' which some readers take to mean he was the first being God created, and therefore not eternal God. That reading has been used to deny his deity.
Explanations: The widely agreed linguistic point is that 'firstborn' in biblical usage often means pre-eminent heir with rights over all, not first in time: Psalm 89 calls David God's firstborn though he was the youngest son. Colossians itself blocks the created reading, saying all things were created by him and he is before all things. The passage is about rank and creatorship, not origin.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 'firstborn' here means supreme heir and creator, not first creature. The passage affirms Christ's deity rather than denying it.
Sources: KJV text on site; biblical firstborn usage including Psalm 89:27; immediate context of Colossians 1:16-17.

Difficulty: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet saying 'The Cretians are alway liars,' then tells Titus to rebuke them sharply. Readers spot a paradox: if all Cretans always lie, then the Cretan prophet lied too, so the statement refutes itself; and the verse also sounds like ethnic stereotyping.
Explanations: The standard resolution is that Paul is quoting a well-known Cretan proverb about a reputation, not stating a literal universal about every Cretan at every moment. A proverbial, hyperbolic saying about a culture's reputation does not create a strict logical paradox, because it is not meant as a formal universal claim. Paul's point is pastoral: false teaching and a lax reputation were real problems in Crete, so Titus must be firm.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Titus 1:12 is a quoted proverb about reputation, not a literal claim about every Cretan and not a licence for stereotyping any people today.
Sources: KJV text on site; recognition of the line as a quoted Cretan saying, as the verse itself states.

Difficulty: Hebrews says Melchizedek was 'without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life.' Readers wonder whether he was a supernatural being, an appearance of Christ, or a man who was never born and never died.
Explanations: The widely held explanation is literary: Genesis records no genealogy, birth, or death for Melchizedek, and Hebrews builds a comparison on that silence. 'Made like unto the Son of God' signals a likeness used for teaching, not an identity claim. His priesthood, unlike Aaron's, is presented without a recorded beginning or end, which makes him a fitting picture of Christ's permanent priesthood.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Hebrews 7 argues from what Genesis does not record, not from Melchizedek being uncreated. He is a historical king-priest used as a type of Christ, not Christ himself under another name.
RelatedTopics: Priesthood; Biblical Interpretation; Superiority of Christ
Sources: KJV text on site; Genesis 14 silence on Melchizedek's genealogy; Psalm 110:4 as cited in Hebrews.

Difficulty: James says God 'cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man,' yet Genesis says God tested Abraham and the Lord's Prayer asks God not to lead us into temptation. Readers ask whether Scripture contradicts itself on whether God tempts or tests.
Explanations: The agreed distinction is between tempting toward evil and testing to prove or strengthen faith. The Greek word covers both, and James is explicit about his sense: God never entices anyone to sin, and sin comes from a person's own desires. Testing, as with Abraham, is a trial with a good purpose, not an enticement to evil. The two uses of one word describe different actions, not a contradiction.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that James 1:13 denies that God entices anyone to sin. It does not deny that God permits or appoints trials that prove faith.
Sources: KJV text on site; Greek range of the tempting/testing word; Genesis 22 as the testing comparison.

Passage: Born of God Does Not Sin
Difficulty: John says 'whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin' and 'cannot sin,' yet in the same letter he says 'if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.' Readers fear this makes every Christian a fraud, or that 1 John contradicts itself within five chapters.
Explanations: The widely agreed grammatical point is that the verbs in 3:6-9 describe ongoing, habitual practice, not a single act: the born-again person does not live in sin as a settled pattern, because God's seed remains in him. Chapter 1 is about honest confession of actual sins; chapter 3 is about direction of life. A Christian still sins and confesses, but does not make sin his home and trade.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 1 John 3:9 describes a changed pattern of life, not sinless perfection. Read with 1:8-10, it promises transformation, not a claim no Christian ever sins.
Sources: KJV text on site; present-tense habitual sense of the verbs in 1 John 3; comparison with 1 John 1:8-10.

Passage: The Johannine Comma: Three That Bear Record in Heaven
Difficulty: John writes 'there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.' Readers who learn this wording is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts ask whether the Trinity has lost its proof text, or whether their Bible has been tampered with.
Explanations: The textual facts are broadly settled: the heavenly-witnesses clause appears in no early Greek manuscript and only in much later Latin copies; it entered some printed Greek texts and from there the King James Version. The earthly witnesses of verse 8, the Spirit, the water, and the blood, are in the early manuscripts. Trinitarian doctrine does not rest on this clause: it is taught across passages such as Matthew 28:19 and John 1:1, which are not in dispute.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that the heavenly-witnesses clause is a later addition and should not be used as a proof text, while the doctrine of the Trinity stands on the wider, well-attested witness of Scripture.
Sources: KJV text on site; manuscript evidence as generally reported (absence from early Greek manuscripts, presence in later Latin copies); no disputed reading relied on.

Passage: Do Not Receive the False Teacher Into Your House
Difficulty: John tells readers not to receive a false teacher into their house or even wish him well, which sounds like a ban on ordinary hospitality or kindness to anyone who disagrees. Readers wonder whether this forbids housing, feeding, or greeting a neighbour with different beliefs.
Explanations: The agreed context is a house church, not a private home's guest room: receiving a travelling teacher into the house meant giving him a platform and endorsing his teaching to the congregation. Refusing that endorsement is not the same as refusing food to a stranger or civility to a neighbour. The letter's concern is partnership with deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh, not everyday kindness.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 2 John 10-11 forbids endorsing and platforming false teachers in the church, not ordinary hospitality or polite conduct toward people of other beliefs.
Sources: KJV text on site; house-church setting of the Johannine letters; verse 7's definition of the deceiver in view.

Passage: A Day Is as a Thousand Years
Difficulty: Peter says 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.' Readers use this as a conversion formula, stretching creation days or prophecy timetables, or they take it to mean God experiences no time at all.
Explanations: The context is patience, not a timetable: Peter is answering scoffers who say Christ's return is delayed, and his point is that God's apparent slowness is longsuffering, giving time for repentance. The day-thousand-years comparison is a simile about God's perspective, drawn from Psalm 90, not an equation to be applied to Genesis days or Revelation's thousand years. It forbids impatience, not careful chronology.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that 2 Peter 3:8 teaches God's patience and perspective, not a day-year conversion chart. It should not be used to re-date creation or the millennium.
RelatedTopics: Second Coming; Patience; Return of Christ
Sources: KJV text on site; Psalm 90:4 as the background simile; immediate context of scoffers and repentance in 2 Peter 3:9.

Passage: Adding to or Taking Away From This Book
Difficulty: Revelation warns that anyone who adds to 'the words of the prophecy of this book' will receive its plagues, and anyone who takes away will lose his part in the book of life. Readers fear that a misquotation, a printing error, or a doubtful reading could cost them salvation.
Explanations: The widely agreed scope is deliberate tampering with the prophecy of Revelation itself, paralleling the warning at the end of Deuteronomy for the law: it addresses those who would falsify God's message, not accidental slips or textual questions. 'This book' in context means Revelation, though the principle of not falsifying Scripture applies more widely. The warning is aimed at the messenger's integrity, not at a reader's imperfect memory.
SiteAssessment: The site's position is that Revelation 22:18-19 warns deliberate falsifiers of the prophecy, not honest readers, translators, or students who wrestle with a difficult text.
Sources: KJV text on site; parallel warning in Deuteronomy 4:2; context of Revelation as a prophetic book.
